questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.challenge_mechanism: The obvious single calculation, dividing input power by the mean rate of temperature rise, gives 960 J/kg/K against an accepted 900, and the item then asks whether that is a discrepancy at all. Separating the two requires a residual plot, which shows the curvature is systematic and the scatter is not, and an uncertainty budget, in which the 6 K rise measured on a 0.5 K scale dominates everything else.

stimulus.title: Measuring the specific heat capacity of aluminium
stimulus.body: A student embedded a $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ electrical heater and a thermometer in an aluminium block of mass $0.500\ \mathrm{kg}$, surrounded the block with lagging, and switched the heater on at $t = 0$. The temperature of the room was $21.0\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$ and stayed constant. She recorded the temperature of the block every $30\ \mathrm{s}$ for five minutes. The thermometer could be read to the nearest $0.5\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$. The heater readings were $V = 12.0 \pm 0.1\ \mathrm{V}$ and $I = 4.00 \pm 0.05\ \mathrm{A}$, and the mass was $0.500 \pm 0.002\ \mathrm{kg}$. The accepted value for aluminium is $900\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

table.caption: Temperature of the block after the heater was switched on

questions.question: The student intended to use $Pt = mc\Delta\theta$ with the whole data set. This question asks you to do the calculation, then to decide whether the data set supports doing it that way at all.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of temperature rise over the first $60\ \mathrm{s}$, and hence determine a value for the specific heat capacity of aluminium. State clearly the assumption your calculation makes about heat loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the uncertainty in your value, combining the uncertainties in the power, the mass and the rate of temperature rise. Identify which contribution dominates and explain in one sentence why.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fit a straight line to all eleven readings and tabulate the residuals. Describe the pattern in them, and state what that pattern establishes about the heat loss from the block.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the anomalous reading, suggest a specific cause that is consistent with the readings either side of it, and state what the student should have done when it occurred. Hence evaluate whether the value from part (a) is consistent with the accepted value.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Over the first $60\ \mathrm{s}$ the temperature rises from $21.0$ to $27.0\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$, so the mean rate is **(M1)**
$$\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}=\frac{6.0}{60}=0.100\ \mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$$
The input power is $P = VI = 12.0 \times 4.00 = 48.0\ \mathrm{W}$. **(A1)** Assuming no energy is lost to the surroundings, $P = mc\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}$, so **(M1)**
$$c=\frac{P}{m(\Delta\theta/\Delta t)}=\frac{48.0}{0.500 \times 0.100}=960\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$$ **(A1)**
The assumption is that all $48\ \mathrm{W}$ goes into the block and none escapes through the lagging.

**(b)** Power: $\dfrac{\delta V}{V}=\dfrac{0.1}{12.0}=0.83\%$ and $\dfrac{\delta I}{I}=\dfrac{0.05}{4.00}=1.25\%$, so $\dfrac{\delta P}{P}=\sqrt{0.83^{2}+1.25^{2}}=1.5\%$. **(A1)** Mass: $\dfrac{0.002}{0.500}=0.4\%$. Rate: each reading carries $\pm 0.5\ \mathrm{K}$, so the rise carries $\sqrt{0.5^{2}+0.5^{2}}=0.71\ \mathrm{K}$ on $6.0\ \mathrm{K}$, which is $11.8\%$. **(M1)(A1)** Combining in quadrature,
$$\frac{\delta c}{c}=\sqrt{1.5^{2}+0.4^{2}+11.8^{2}}=11.9\%$$
so $\delta c \approx 110\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $c = 960 \pm 110\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. **(A1)** The rate dominates, because a $6\ \mathrm{K}$ rise is only twelve times the resolution of the thermometer while the other two quantities are measured to better than $2\%$.

**(c)** The least-squares line is $\theta = 0.0817\,t + 22.0$. **(A1)** The residuals, in the order of the table, are
$$-1.02,\ -0.47,\ +0.08,\ +0.63,\ +0.68,\ +0.73,\ +0.78,\ +0.33,\ -1.12,\ -0.07,\ -0.52$$
**(M1)(A1)** Setting aside the $240\ \mathrm{s}$ point, they rise from about $-1.0$ to $+0.8$ and fall back to about $-0.5$: a smooth arch rather than scatter. That is the signature of a systematic effect. The data are concave downwards, meaning the rate of rise decreases with time, and that is exactly what a loss rate proportional to $(\theta - \theta_{\text{room}})$ produces while the input power stays constant. Random error alone would give residuals of alternating sign with no trend. **(A1)**

**(d)** The anomalous reading is at $t = 240\ \mathrm{s}$: $40.5\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$, which is about $1.3\ \mathrm{K}$ below the value expected from the readings at $210\ \mathrm{s}$ and $270\ \mathrm{s}$. **(A1)** The next reading returns to the smooth trend, so the curve was not permanently displaced; a genuine extra loss of heat would have lowered every later reading, not just one. A cause consistent with that is that the thermometer probe was disturbed or pulled slightly out of its hole at that moment, so it briefly read closer to the temperature of the air. **(A1)** The probe should have been clamped and its seating checked before the run, and any disturbance logged at the time; if one occurred, the run should be repeated rather than the point removed afterwards. Finally, $960 \pm 110$ contains $900$, so the result is consistent with the accepted value; the value is high, in the direction the residual analysis predicts, because heat loss reduces the measured rate of rise. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Accept $0.100\ \mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$ and $960\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$; the assumption mark is separate and should not be given for 'heat losses are negligible' written without reference to the interval used. (b) Accept any combined uncertainty between $9\%$ and $14\%$; the mark scheme is checking that the candidate identifies the temperature difference as dominant and says why. A candidate who adds the percentage uncertainties linearly rather than in quadrature is being conservative and should not be penalised. (c) The residuals need not be tabulated to two decimals; the mark is for the shape. Accept 'the residuals are positive in the middle and negative at both ends' as the description, and require the word systematic or an equivalent. Do not credit 'the graph is curved' on its own, since that is the observation and not the inference. (d) Accept any cause that predicts a single-point dip followed by a return to trend; specifically reject friction-style answers that would displace all later points. The consistency judgement must quote the uncertainty interval, not just say 'close enough'.
questions.explanation:
This item is built around a trap that catches good students as often as weak ones. The natural calculation gives $960$ against an accepted $900$, which looks like a $7\%$ error, and the instinct is to hunt for the mistake. There is no mistake. The uncertainty on the value is about $12\%$, almost all of it from measuring a $6\ \mathrm{K}$ rise with a thermometer that reads to the nearest half degree, so $960$ and $900$ are the same number to within the resolution of the apparatus. Recognising that requires an uncertainty budget, which is why part (b) is worth four marks on its own.

The residual plot in part (c) then supplies what the uncertainty budget cannot: it says something about the *direction* of the error, not just its size. A student who is told that heat loss makes the measured rate too small will usually repeat it as a fact. A student who plots the residuals sees the arch, sees that it is systematic rather than random, and can then say which way the error pushes and why — the loss rate grows as the block gets hotter while the input power does not. That is the difference between knowing a correction and being able to tell whether it applies to a particular data set.

Part (d) closes the loop by asking a question that is really about the shape of the data rather than the size of the numbers. The $240\ \mathrm{s}$ reading is low, but the $270\ \mathrm{s}$ reading is back on trend, and that single fact eliminates most of the obvious explanations. A disturbance to the probe is consistent with it; a genuine change in the heat loss is not, because that would have moved the whole tail of the curve. The same reasoning is what makes the prescribed action a repeat rather than a deletion: the point carries information about what went wrong, and deleting it afterwards throws that away while leaving the run just as compromised as it was.

provenance.adaptation: Original item. The dataset was generated in Python from the lumped-capacity model d(theta)/dt = (P - k(theta - theta_room))/(mc) with m = 0.500 kg, c = 900 J/kg/K, k = 0.8 W/K, P = 48 W and theta_room = 21 C, then rounded to the 0.5 C resolution of the thermometer; the anomalous point was seeded afterwards. The residual arch, the uncertainty budget and the 960-vs-900 comparison all follow from that model rather than being chosen.

verification.method: Dataset generated in Python from the lumped-capacity heat-loss model and rounded to the instrument resolution; the least-squares line, all eleven residuals, the percentage uncertainty budget and the interpolated value at 240 s were recomputed and compared with the values quoted in the answer.
solution_skeleton: take the mean rate of temperature rise over an early interval where loss is smallest
convert the input power and the rate into a specific heat capacity using P = mc dT/dt
build a percentage uncertainty budget and identify which term dominates
fit a straight line to the whole run and read the shape of the residuals to separate systematic curvature from scatter
test a candidate cause for the outlier against the readings either side of it before accepting it

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.challenge_mechanism: Two different faults are seeded and they are not the same kind of fault. A constant zero error on the travelling microscope shifts every point equally and therefore leaves the gradient, and the wavelength, untouched; a miscounted fringe spacing at one slit separation scales a single point and does move the gradient. Distinguishing the two, and saying which one has to be dealt with, is the whole question.

stimulus.title: Measuring the wavelength of laser light with a double slit
stimulus.body: A student directed a laser at a double slit and measured the fringe separation $s$ on a screen $L = 2.000\ \mathrm{m}$ away, for seven different slit separations $d$. For each Separation she used a travelling microscope to measure the distance across ten fringe spacings and then divided by ten. The microscope could be read to the nearest $0.01\ \mathrm{mm}$, and the student quoted each value of $s$ to $0.01\ \mathrm{mm}$ with an estimated uncertainty of $\pm 0.02\ \mathrm{mm}$, which she judged to be dominated by locating the centre of a fringe rather than by reading the scale. The theory predicts $s = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$.

table.caption: Fringe separation for seven slit separations, screen distance $L = 2.000\ \mathrm{m}$

questions.question: The data do not lie on a straight line when $s$ is plotted against $d$, and one point does not lie on the line even after the axes are chosen correctly. Both facts matter, and they have different consequences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the student should plot in order to obtain a straight-line graph, state what the gradient of that line represents, and explain why plotting $s$ against $d$ would not be helpful.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Tabulate values of $1/d$ and plot $s$ against $1/d$. Determine the gradient of the best-fit line and hence determine the wavelength of the laser light. Estimate the uncertainty in the wavelength by drawing the steepest and the shallowest straight lines consistent with the error bars on the plotted points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the intercept of your line on the $s$ axis and hence determine the zero error of the travelling microscope, explaining how a zero error on the instrument relates to the intercept of this graph.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the anomalous row, show quantitatively that your suggested cause accounts for the recorded value, state what the student should have done when it occurred, and state whether the zero error from part (c) affects the value of the wavelength.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Since $s = \lambda L/d$, the student should plot $s$ against $1/d$. **(M1)** The gradient of the resulting straight line is $\lambda L$, so $\lambda$ is the gradient divided by $L$. **(A1)** Plotting $s$ against $d$ gives a curve of the form $s \propto 1/d$, from which a gradient cannot be read and an intercept cannot be interpreted. **(A1)**

**(b)** Tabulating $1/d$ in $\mathrm{mm^{-1}}$: $2.500,\ 2.000,\ 1.667,\ 1.250,\ 1.000,\ 0.800,\ 0.500$. **(A1)** The first point lies well above the line through the others, so it is excluded from the fit; the remaining six give a gradient of **(M1)**
$$\text{gradient} = 1.27\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}$$
**(A1)** Converting, $1.27\ \mathrm{mm^{2}} = 1.27 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}$, and **(M1)**
$$\lambda = \frac{1.27 \times 10^{-6}}{2.000} = 6.33 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = 633\ \mathrm{nm}$$
**(A1)** For the uncertainty, the steepest line consistent with the error bars passes through $(0.500,\,0.66)$ and $(2.000,\,2.60)$, giving a gradient of $1.293\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}$, and the shallowest passes through $(0.500,\,0.70)$ and $(2.000,\,2.56)$, giving $1.240\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}$. **(M1)** The half-range is $0.027\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}$, so **(A1)**
$$\delta\lambda = \frac{0.027 \times 10^{-6}}{2.000} = 1.3 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$$
and $\lambda = 633 \pm 13\ \mathrm{nm}$. This is about $2\%$, and it is far larger than the scatter of the points about the line, which tells the student that the precision is limited by locating the fringes rather than by random scatter.

**(c)** The best-fit line through the six good points has an intercept of about $+0.05\ \mathrm{mm}$. **(A1)** Each value of $s$ was obtained by measuring a distance $D$ across ten spacings and dividing by ten. If the microscope has a zero error $e$, then $D_{\text{meas}} = 10\,s_{\text{true}} + e$, so **(M1)**
$$s_{\text{meas}} = s_{\text{true}} + \frac{e}{10}$$
The intercept is therefore $e/10$, giving $e = 0.05 \times 10 = +0.50\ \mathrm{mm}$. **(A1)** The microscope read $0.50\ \mathrm{mm}$ too high on every setting of the crosswire; that is, it did not read zero when the crosswire was at the reference mark.

**(d)** The anomalous row is $d = 0.40\ \mathrm{mm}$, where $s = 3.53\ \mathrm{mm}$; the line predicts $3.21\ \mathrm{mm}$. **(A1)** If the student had counted eleven spacings on that row but still divided by ten, then **(M1)**
$$s = \frac{11 \times 3.164 + 0.50}{10} = \frac{34.80 + 0.50}{10} = 3.53\ \mathrm{mm}$$
which reproduces the recorded value exactly. **(A1)** She should have re-counted the fringes and re-measured at the time, and recorded how many spacings each measurement covered; crossing out the point afterwards is not acceptable, and leaving it in the fit raises the gradient by about $9\%$ and gives $\lambda \approx 692\ \mathrm{nm}$. **(A1)** The zero error does not affect the wavelength: it adds the same constant to every value of $s$, so it moves the intercept and leaves the gradient, and hence $\lambda$, unchanged.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Accept 'plot s against the reciprocal of d'; the mark for the gradient is for stating $\lambda L$ and not just $\lambda$. (b) Accept gradients from $1.25$ to $1.29\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}$ and wavelengths from $625$ to $645\ \mathrm{nm}$, provided the excluded point is named. A candidate who includes all seven points gets about $692\ \mathrm{nm}$ and should lose the gradient mark but can still earn the conversion mark on follow-through. (c) Accept intercepts from $0.03$ to $0.07\ \mathrm{mm}$ and zero errors from $0.3$ to $0.7\ \mathrm{mm}$; the reasoning that the intercept is one tenth of the zero error is the point, so credit it even if the arithmetic slips. (d) The quantitative check is what distinguishes an answer from a guess: a candidate must show that the eleven-for-ten count reproduces $3.53\ \mathrm{mm}$, and other causes should only be credited if they too are tested against the number. The final statement about the zero error must be a conclusion about the gradient, not an assertion that zero errors never matter. The uncertainty in (b) must come from the extreme-lines construction rather than from a formula the candidate has memorised; accept a half-range anywhere from $0.02$ to $0.04\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}$ and wavelengths quoted as $633 \pm 10$ to $633 \pm 20\ \mathrm{nm}$. The observation at the end, that the error bars give a larger uncertainty than the scatter does, is the point of the exercise and should be credited if offered.
questions.explanation:
The design of this item rests on a distinction that students find genuinely hard: not all experimental faults are the same kind of thing, and they do not all damage the result equally. A zero error on the travelling microscope adds the same amount to every distance reading, so it shifts the whole data set up by a constant and leaves the gradient untouched. Because the wavelength is obtained from the gradient, the wavelength survives the zero error completely intact. Students who have learned 'systematic errors invalidate the experiment' will say the opposite, and part (c) is built to catch exactly that.

The miscounted fringe spacing is the other kind of fault. It multiplies one row by a factor rather than adding a constant to all of them, so it does move the gradient, and it moves it a long way: including the bad point gives $\lambda \approx 692\ \mathrm{nm}$ instead of $633\ \mathrm{nm}$, an error of about $9\%$ from a single row out of seven. That is the more damaging fault, and it is the one that is easy to miss, because the point does not look obviously absurd on its own.

This is also why part (d) asks for a quantitative check rather than a plausible story. Plenty of causes could be invented for a point that sits high, and most of them would be wrong. The eleven-for-ten count does not merely sound plausible: it produces $3.53\ \mathrm{mm}$ to the last quoted digit, and no other simple account does. Requiring the candidate to show that arithmetic turns the item from an exercise in imagination into an exercise in evidence, which is the habit the data-based question exists to test. The final clause, about re-measuring rather than deleting, follows from the same principle: the point is evidence of what went wrong, and the right response to evidence is to go back and check, not to remove it.

provenance.adaptation: Original item. The dataset was generated in Python from s = lambda*L/d with lambda = 632.8 nm and L = 2.000 m, a constant zero error of +0.50 mm applied to every distance reading (giving an intercept of +0.05 mm on s), and a miscount of eleven spacings for ten seeded into the d = 0.40 mm row; the value 3.53 mm emerges from that model rather than being chosen. The two-fault structure, one additive and one multiplicative, is the reason the pair was seeded together.

verification.method: Dataset generated in Python from s = lambda*L/d with the seeded zero error and the seeded miscount; least-squares gradients computed both with and without the anomalous row, and the eleven-for-ten hypothesis checked against the recorded value to the quoted precision. The uncertainty in the gradient was recomputed from the two extreme lines through the +/-0.02 mm error bars at the ends of the plotted range, and compared with the standard error of the least-squares gradient, which is smaller by an order of magnitude.
solution_skeleton: linearise the reciprocal relationship by plotting the fringe separation against the reciprocal of the slit separation
exclude the row that does not follow the line and take the gradient of the remainder
convert the gradient into a wavelength using the screen distance and the units of the axes
interpret the intercept as the constant zero error divided by the number of spacings measured
test a multiplicative cause for the outlier against the recorded value before accepting it, and say whether each fault moves the gradient

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.challenge_mechanism: The resonant frequency and the peak amplitude can both be read straight off the table and neither of them characterises the resonance, which is the point. Characterising it requires the width at 1/sqrt(2) of the peak, and that has to be interpolated from two points on each side where the curve is steepest, so the answer depends on drawing a smooth curve rather than reading numbers. One row is far off that curve for a reason the candidate has to name.

stimulus.title: How sharp is the resonance of a driven mass-spring system?
stimulus.body: A student drove a mass-spring system vertically with a vibration generator whose frequency she could set, and recorded the steady-state amplitude of oscillation with a position sensor. She kept the amplitude of the driving motion constant throughout and checked it on an oscilloscope before each reading. The sensor could be read to the nearest $0.01\ \mathrm{mm}$, and the student estimated the uncertainty in a single amplitude reading as $\pm 0.05\ \mathrm{mm}$ because the trace never settled completely. She intended to characterise the resonance by more than its position.

table.caption: Steady-state amplitude of oscillation at each driving frequency

questions.question: Two quantities describe this system: the frequency at which it responds most strongly, and how sharply it responds. The table gives the first directly. The second has to be extracted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plot the data. Determine the resonant frequency and the maximum amplitude, explaining how you obtained them and why the resonant frequency is not simply the frequency of the largest recorded amplitude.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the two frequencies at which the amplitude has fallen to $A_{\max}/\sqrt{2}$, and hence determine the quality factor $Q$ of the system using $Q = f_{0}/\Delta f$, where $\Delta f$ is the width of the resonance at those two frequencies.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the quality factor measures about the system, and why a system with a large $Q$ takes a long time to stop oscillating once the driver is switched off.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the anomalous row, suggest a specific cause consistent with the readings either side of it, and state what the student should have done when it occurred.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The peak of the curve lies at $52\ \mathrm{Hz}$, where the amplitude is $12.00\ \mathrm{mm}$. **(A1)(A1)** The resonant frequency is the frequency at the maximum of a smooth curve drawn through the points, so it is found from the graph and not by picking the largest tabulated value; with readings every $2\ \mathrm{Hz}$ near the peak, the true maximum could lie anywhere between about $51$ and $53\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and the data as recorded cannot locate it more closely than that. **(M1)(A1)** Reading the largest tabulated amplitude gives the same number here only because a reading happens to sit at the top of the curve, and that is luck rather than method.

**(b)** $A_{\max}/\sqrt{2} = 12.00/1.414 = 8.49\ \mathrm{mm}$. **(A1)** Drawing a smooth curve through the points and reading off where it crosses $8.49\ \mathrm{mm}$, the lower crossing is at about $50.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and the upper at about $53.8\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **(M1)(A1)(A1)** Hence **(M1)**
$$\Delta f = 53.8 - 50.0 = 3.8\ \mathrm{Hz},\qquad Q = \frac{52}{3.8} \approx 14$$
**(A1)** Since both crossings have to be interpolated on the steepest part of the curve, the value is good to about two significant figures.

**(c)** $Q$ measures how sharply the system responds: it is a ratio of the energy stored in the oscillation to the energy lost per cycle, and it is large when the damping is light. **(A1)** A lightly damped system loses only a small fraction of its energy each cycle, so it needs many cycles before the amplitude has fallen appreciably. **(A1)** Quantitatively the amplitude decays as $e^{-\pi f_{0} t/Q}$, so the decay time is proportional to $Q$: this system rings on for roughly $Q$ radians of oscillation divided into $\pi f_{0}$, that is, of order $Q/f_{0}$ seconds, rather than stopping within a cycle or two. **(A1)**

**(d)** The anomalous row is $f = 72\ \mathrm{Hz}$, where the amplitude is $2.10\ \mathrm{mm}$. The readings either side are $1.39\ \mathrm{mm}$ at $66\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $0.63\ \mathrm{mm}$ at $80\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so a smooth curve through them would give about $0.93\ \mathrm{mm}$ at $72\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and the recorded value is more than twice that. **(A1)** Since the student reports having checked the drive amplitude before each reading, the most likely cause is that the output control on the signal generator was disturbed after that check, so the driving amplitude was larger for that one reading; a mains-frequency pickup would not produce a spike at $72\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **(A1)** She should have re-checked the drive amplitude, seen that it had changed, and re-taken the reading immediately; if that was not possible, the point should be excluded and the exclusion recorded in the log, not quietly dropped from the graph. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Accept $52\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $12.00\ \mathrm{mm}$. The explanation mark is for the point that the tabulated maximum is not the resonant frequency in general; a candidate who says the two are the same because the largest reading happens to be at the peak has not answered. (b) Accept $A_{\max}/\sqrt{2} = 8.49\ \mathrm{mm}$, crossings anywhere in $49.9$ to $50.3\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $53.5$ to $54.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and $Q$ from $13$ to $15$. Do not penalise a candidate who reads the crossings from a straight-line interpolation between adjacent points and gets $14.1$; note in feedback that the curve is not straight there and that linear interpolation is an approximation. (c) Accept any correct statement about the ratio of stored to lost energy per cycle; the mark for the decay is for linking the long ring-down to the small fractional loss, and a candidate who simply asserts that a large $Q$ rings for longer has not explained. (d) The cause must be tested against the number: credit any suggestion that would raise one reading while leaving its neighbours alone, and reject friction or damping answers, which would move the whole curve rather than one point.
questions.explanation:
The reason this item exists is that the two numbers a student can read straight off the table are the two that matter least. The resonant frequency and the peak amplitude say where the system responds and how strongly, but they say nothing about how selective that response is, and selectivity is what distinguishes a useful resonator from a useless one. A bell and a bowl of jelly can share a resonant frequency; what separates them is the width of the peak. Getting at the width requires the half-power points, which sit on the steepest part of the curve where interpolation is hardest, so the item forces the candidate to draw the curve rather than read the table.

The choice of $A_{\max}/\sqrt{2}$ rather than $A_{\max}/2$ is worth dwelling on in teaching, because it is the one place where the factor of two is routinely misplaced. Power is proportional to amplitude squared, so halving the power means dividing the amplitude by $\sqrt{2}$, not by $2$. Using $A_{\max}/2$ would give a wider interval, a larger $\Delta f$ and a smaller $Q$, and the error is invisible in the working because every step afterwards is correct. Part (b) is worth five marks largely because of that one factor.

Part (d) asks for a cause and then quietly requires it to be checked. The point at $72\ \mathrm{Hz}$ sits above its neighbours, and the tempting answer is to say the resonance is broad or that there is a second mode. Neither works: a second resonance would raise the readings around $72\ \mathrm{Hz}$, not just the one, and a broader peak would lift $66\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $80\ \mathrm{Hz}$ too. Only something that acts on that single reading will do, and the item supplies the clue by telling the candidate that the drive amplitude was checked before each reading but not after. The deeper lesson is about experimental bookkeeping: a control that is verified before a measurement but not after it is only half checked, and the row that gives the game away is the one nobody was looking at, far off resonance where the amplitude is small and the error is proportionally large.

provenance.adaptation: Original item. The dataset was generated in Python from the standard driven-oscillator response A proportional to 1/sqrt((1 - (f/f0)^2)^2 + (f/(Q f0))^2) with f0 = 52 Hz and Q = 14, scaled so the peak amplitude is 12.00 mm, and rounded to the 0.01 mm resolution of the sensor; the anomalous value at 72 Hz was seeded afterwards. The true half-power width from the model is 3.72 Hz, so the reading from the graph, 3.8 Hz, is honest about the precision a student can actually achieve.

verification.method: Dataset generated in Python from the driven-oscillator response function and rounded to the sensor resolution; the half-power frequencies located by bisection on the generating model (50.04 Hz and 53.76 Hz, giving Q = 13.96) and compared with the value obtainable from the tabulated points by interpolation (Q = 14.1), and the 72 Hz row checked against the neighbouring readings.
solution_skeleton: draw a smooth resonance curve and locate its maximum rather than quoting the largest tabulated amplitude
convert the maximum amplitude to the half-power level by dividing by the square root of two
read both half-power frequencies from the curve and take their difference as the bandwidth
divide the resonant frequency by the bandwidth to obtain the quality factor
relate the quality factor to the fractional energy loss per cycle and hence to the ring-down time
test a candidate cause for the outlying row against its neighbours rather than against the peak
